extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of social psychology, political scientists, policymakers, general readers interested in crowd behavior
extracted.subtask_description: Classifying and describing different kinds of crowds and their psychological characteristics, with attention to implications for press, governments, juries, and collective criminal acts. Focus is on how crowds form opinions, act, and are influenced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Powerlessness of governments to direct opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: A phenomenon quite new: the powerlessness of governments to direct opinion; statesmen no longer direct opinion but endeavour to follow it and often adopt an unstable line of conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Causes cited: increasing power of crowds, extreme mobility of ideas, and the newspaper press presenting contrary opinions; consequence is that governments fear public opinion and follow it rather than lead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Press as reflection, not director, of opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: The press, which formerly directed opinion, has had to humble itself before the power of crowds and 'become a mere agency for the supply of information.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because of competition and the need to retain readers, the press follows changes in public thought, renounces enforcing an idea or doctrine, suppresses extensive literary criticism, and concentrates on close watching of the course of opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ephemeral and highly mobile modern opinions
rubrics_metrics.description: The extreme mobility of ideas and the newspaper press result in contrary opinions continually being brought before crowds, so 'no opinion succeeds in becoming widespread' and 'an opinion nowadays dies out before it has found a sufficiently wide acceptance to become general.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This mobility leads to the powerlessness of governments and the press to fix opinion; it also makes public sentiment changeable and often superficial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Close monitoring of public opinion as principal preoccupation
rubrics_metrics.description: The close watching of the course of opinion has become to-day the principal preoccupation of the press and of governments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: They must continually know the effect produced by events, proposals, and speeches, because 'nothing is more mobile and changeable than the thought of crowds.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Modern crowds' indifference to general beliefs
rubrics_metrics.description: Total absence of direction of opinion and destruction of general beliefs result in extreme divergency of convictions and growing indifference of crowds to everything not plainly touching their immediate interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Doctrinal questions (e.g., socialism) only recruit genuine champions among the quite illiterate classes; the lower middle class and semi-educated workers become sceptical or unstable in opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of crowds (heterogeneous vs homogeneous)
rubrics_metrics.description: General division of crowds into: A. Heterogeneous crowds (anonymous crowds like street crowds; crowds not anonymous like juries, parliamentary assemblies) and B. Homogeneous crowds (sects, castes, classes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Heterogeneous crowds are composed of individuals of any description; homogeneous crowds include groups united by belief (sects), profession/status (castes), or interests/habits (classes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of race (spirit of the race) in crowd behaviour
rubrics_metrics.description: The spirit of the race is a fundamental factor determining the character of crowds: 'THE INFERIOR CHARACTERISTICS OF CROWDS ARE THE LESS ACCENTUATED IN PROPORTION AS THE SPIRIT OF THE RACE IS STRONG.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Crowds composed chiefly of a single race will show consistent dispositions (e.g., Latin crowds favor centralisation; English/American crowds favor private initiative). Strong racial collective spirit limits the unreflecting power of crowds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Difference between anonymous and non-anonymous crowds
rubrics_metrics.description: Anonymous crowds (street crowds) lack a sentiment of responsibility, while crowds not anonymous (juries, assemblies) develop responsibility, producing different tendencies in their acts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The presence or absence of responsibility influences how a crowd behaves and the degree to which individuals feel accountable.

rubrics_metrics.name: General psychological characteristics of heterogeneous crowds
rubrics_metrics.description: Heterogeneous crowds: composed of individuals of any description; when assembled, collective psychology differs from individual psychology—intelligence is without influence; they are under the sway of unconscious sentiments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key features include openness to suggestion, credulity, mobility, exaggeration of sentiments (good or bad), and certain rudimentary forms of morality. Race modifies these but does not eliminate them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criminal acts of crowds are driven by suggestion and unconsciousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Because crowds after excitement enter an automatic and unconscious state guided by suggestion, it is difficult to qualify them psychologically as criminal in the ordinary sense; individuals often believe they have acted from duty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples (e.g., murder of the Bastille governor, September massacres) show obedience to collective suggestions, collective approval that validates the act for participants, and behaviour resembling that of instinct-driven animals rather than reflective criminals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rudimentary collective justice and reasoning in crowds
rubrics_metrics.description: Crowds often form improvised tribunals and use simple criteria (profession, appearance, reputation) to judge guilt; reasoning is rudimentary and collective decisions can authorize mass violence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The crowd's conception of justice justifies wholesale judgments (e.g., slaughter of nobles without individual trial) and uses outward signs as proxies for guilt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coexistence of contradictory sentiments within crowds
rubrics_metrics.description: Crowds can simultaneously exhibit extreme ferocity and extreme tenderness (e.g., embracing an acquitted prisoner and then resuming massacre), showing complex, fluctuating moral responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This instability means crowds may alternate between cruelty and sympathy, and their actions reflect swings of sentiment rather than consistent moral reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independence of jury verdicts from juror composition
rubrics_metrics.description: Statistics show that jury decisions are independent of their composition; varying the social/intellectual makeup of juries has little effect on verdict outcomes: 'ITS VERDICTS HAVE REMAINED THE SAME.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attempts to select more 'enlightened' jurors do not materially change verdicts, indicating the collective dynamics of juries dominate individual juror attributes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Juries are guided by sentiment and prestige rather than argument
rubrics_metrics.description: Juries are strongly impressed by sentimental considerations, pity, and the appearance or prestige of the accused; they are very slightly influenced by pure argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: They respond to displays (a mother nursing, orphans), to agreeable appearance, and to prestige (name, birth, wealth, celebrity, illustrious counsel). They tend to be indulgent for passion-motivated crimes and severe for crimes deemed dangerous to society.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective counsel strategy for juries: persuade feelings and leaders
rubrics_metrics.description: The chief concern of a good counsel should be to work upon the feelings of the jury, argue little, identify the 'leading spirits' among jurors and win them over; adapt language in real time to jurors' reactions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Oratory must observe jurors, secure adhesion of already favourable members, then turn to refractory members to discover motives of hostility. One or two energetic men suffice to carry the rest; tactics include pleasing influential jurors and adjusting speech dynamically.

rubrics_metrics.name: The jury as a tempering institution vis-à-vis magistrates
rubrics_metrics.description: The jury alone can temper the severity of the law by taking account of particular cases and pity; replacing juries with magistrates risks losing this mitigating function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While juries commit errors, many of those errors originate with magistrates; juries provide the accused a chance against a judicial caste and intuitively differentiate crimes dangerous to society from those less so.
